title: The vow that named Bhishma
hookLine: Devavrata vows lifelong brahmacharya and the sky calls him Bhishma: a vow chosen, not forced
carry: brahmacharya: a vow chosen, not forced
last: A SACRED VOW IS SPOKEN BEFORE WITNESSES.

cards: The fisherman is a careful man. He has just heard the heir to the throne give up his crown, in front of witnesses, for a grandson who isn't born yet. He believes him.
He says so. And then he keeps thinking, out loud, while the elders listen. You'll keep your word, he says.
But you'll have sons one day. Will they keep it? A promise is only as strong as the people who inherit it.

teach.h: I'LL SETTLE THE MATTER OF MY CHILDREN.
teach.b: Devavrata answers him before the chiefs. I've already given up the kingdom, he says. Now I'll settle the matter of my children.
From today, I take up brahmacharya, a vow of celibacy, for the rest of my life. And then, in the text's sense: even if I die without a son, I'll still reach the heavenly worlds.
The fisherman is shaken; the text says the hair on his body stood on end. I give her, he says. And the sky answers.

Gods, celestial dancers and sages rain flowers on Devavrata's head and cry out a name: this one is Bhishma. In Ganguli's English the name is glossed with one word: terrible. A vow so hard it's frightening.
From now on the story calls him Bhishma, after what he promised.
Brahmacharya is a real Hindu discipline. It's the first of the four stages of life, the student years, kept while you learn; and many Hindu monks keep it for life, to give everything to God.
Bhishma takes it for his father. The Vasus foretold he'd have no children, and Vasishtha's curse said so too, but here nobody forces it on him. He chooses it, freely, out loud.
In Hindi, a Bhishma pratigya, a Bhishma vow, means a promise nothing can break.
And because he had no children to offer him water after his death, on Bhishma Ashtami many Hindus offer it for him themselves.

how: Brahmacharya, celibacy and self-restraint, is the discipline of the student stage of life in Hindu tradition, and many Hindu monks keep it for life. On Bhishma Ashtami, some Hindus offer water (tarpana) for Bhishma, who had no children to do it.

practice: For this sit, make one small vow, only to yourself: I'll stay still until the bell. When you want to shift or check something, notice the wanting and stay, and if you move, simply begin the vow again.
A small promise kept all the way through is still a promise kept.
